definition: Software that records every change to a set of files over time, who made it and why, so a team can work in parallel, review changes and return to any earlier state. Git is the most widely used version control system.
A project tracked by Git: the working files plus the hidden .git directory that holds every object, ref and setting. Cloning copies a repository, including its history.

Storing data under a key computed from the data itself (a hash), rather than under a name or location you choose. Identical content always gets the same key, and changing any byte changes the key. Git's object store works this way.
example: A file containing hello plus a newline is stored by Git under ce013625… in every repository in the world.

definition: One item in Git's database: a blob, tree, commit or annotated tag. Each object has a type, a size and content, is named by the hash of those, and never changes once written.
Git's object type for file contents: just the bytes of one version of a file, with no name, permissions or timestamp. Two files with identical bytes share one blob.
example: Copying hello.txt to copy.txt adds no new blob, because the content is identical.

definition: Git's object type for a directory listing. Each entry gives a mode, a type (blob or tree), a hash and a name, so trees are where file and directory names are stored.
A commit with no parent, usually the first commit in a repository. A repository can have several, for example after merging in an unrelated project.

In Git, a snapshot of the whole project recorded as an object: it points at one root tree and its parent commits, and stores the author, committer, timestamps and message. To commit is to create one from the staging area.
example: git commit -m "Fix typo" writes a new commit whose parent is the previous tip of the branch.

definition: The commit (or commits) a commit was built on, recorded by hash inside it. A normal commit has one parent and a merge commit has two or more; following parents backwards gives the history.
A commit with two or more parents, created when Git joins two lines of history. Its first parent is the branch you were on and its second is the branch you merged in.

The first parent recorded in a merge commit: the branch that was checked out when the merge was made. git log --first-parent follows only first parents, giving a mainline view that skips the internals of merged branches.
Two identities Git stores in every commit: the author wrote the change, the committer last applied it. Rebase and cherry-pick normally keep the author but record a new committer and commit time.

A Git tag stored as a real object, with its own tagger, date, message and optional signature, plus a ref under refs/tags pointing at that object. Recommended for releases; plain git describe only uses annotated tags.
example: git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release" writes one new tag object.

definition: A Git tag that is only a ref pointing straight at an object, usually a commit, with no tag object, message or tagger. Cheap, but ignored by plain git describe.
example: git tag v0.1 writes no object; git cat-file -t v0.1 prints commit.

definition: A named ref under refs/tags that marks a particular commit, typically a release such as v2.1.0. Tags are meant to stay fixed, but anyone with push rights can move one, so treat published tags as immutable by policy.

A cryptographic hash function producing a 160-bit (20-byte) value, printed as 40 hexadecimal characters. Git names objects with SHA-1 by default; it is broken for collision resistance, so Git uses a hardened variant (SHA-1DC).

A cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family producing a 256-bit (32-byte) value, printed as 64 hexadecimal characters. Git supports it as an alternative object format and plans to make it the default in Git 3.0.
example: git init --object-format=sha256 creates a SHA-256 repository.

definition: A hardened SHA-1 implementation that detects the known collision-attack patterns and refuses them, while giving normal SHA-1 results for ordinary data. Git has used it by default since version 2.13.
The 2017 attack by Google and CWI Amsterdam that produced the first public SHA-1 collision: two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash.

The hash that names a Git object, such as ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a. People often call it the SHA after the hash function. Git accepts any unique prefix, so abbreviations of 7 or more characters are common.
Base 16: a way of writing numbers with the digits 0–9 and the letters a–f. Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so one byte is two hex digits.
example: The byte 255 is ff in hexadecimal.

definition: The byte with value 0. Git puts one after the header of every object, between the text "type size" and the content, to mark where the header ends.
Two different inputs that produce the same hash value. If an attacker can create one on purpose, they could swap one Git object for another with the same name.
The property of a cryptographic hash function that it is practically impossible to find two different inputs with the same output. Git's tamper evidence depends on it.

A structure where each node is named by a hash that covers the hashes of the nodes it points to, so changing any leaf changes every hash above it. Git's commits and trees form one, which makes history tamper-evident.
Directed acyclic graph: nodes joined by one-way arrows with no loops. Git history is a DAG of commits, each pointing back at its parents.
An append-only ledger in which each block includes the hash of the previous block, so altering an old block breaks every later link. It uses the same hash-chaining idea as Git history.
A public, append-only log of issued TLS certificates, built on a Merkle tree so anyone can check that entries were never altered or removed.
A human-readable name that points at a Git object by its hash, such as refs/heads/main or refs/tags/v1.0. Branches, tags and remote-tracking branches are all refs.
In Git, a ref under refs/heads that names one commit, the tip of a line of work. Committing moves it forward. The git branch command lists, creates or deletes these refs without copying any files.
example: git branch feature creates a ref naming the current commit; no objects are written.

definition: Git's pointer to what you have checked out. Normally it is a symbolic ref naming the current branch (ref: refs/heads/main); new commits move that branch. Detached, it holds a commit hash directly.
A ref that points at another ref rather than at an object. HEAD is the usual example: it names the current branch.
A local ref such as origin/main, under refs/remotes, recording where a branch on a remote repository was when you last fetched or pushed. You do not commit to it directly.
Another copy of the repository that yours exchanges commits with, usually on a hosting service, named origin by default.

The state where HEAD holds a commit hash instead of a branch name, for example after checking out a tag or hash. New commits made then belong to no branch and become unreachable once you switch away, unless you create a branch.
A branch that HEAD names but that has no commit yet, as in a freshly created repository before the first commit.
A single file, .git/packed-refs, into which Git gathers many refs to avoid thousands of tiny files. Scripts should read refs through git rev-parse or git for-each-ref, not the files.
An alternative storage format for refs, designed to stay fast with very large numbers of refs. Use Git commands rather than relying on its on-disk layout.
Git's index: the file .git/index listing the paths, modes and blob hashes that will form the next commit. git add stages a file's current content there; git commit turns it into a tree.
The ordinary files you see and edit, checked out from a commit. Changes there are not recorded until you stage and commit them.
The command that stages a file: it stores the file's current content as a blob and records that blob's hash in the staging area for the next commit.
The command that shows what has changed in the working tree and staging area compared with the last commit, and which branch HEAD is on.
The command that shows line-by-line differences between two snapshots, such as the working tree and the staging area, or two commits. Git computes diffs on demand; it does not store commits as diffs.
A low-level command that prints a Git object: -t shows its type and -p shows its content in readable form.
example: git cat-file -p HEAD prints the current commit's tree, parent, author and message.

definition: A low-level command that computes the object ID a file would have as a blob, and with -w writes it into the object store.
A low-level command that turns the current staging area into tree objects and prints the root tree's hash.
The command that changes which branch is checked out (git switch -c creates one first). It updates HEAD, the staging area and the working tree.

An older all-purpose command that switches branches or restores files; git switch and git restore split those jobs. During merges and rebases, git checkout --ours or --theirs picks one side of a conflicted file.
A command that turns any name Git understands (a branch, tag, HEAD~3, an abbreviated hash) into a full object ID. Scripts use it instead of reading ref files.
A command that lists refs and their targets in a chosen format, independent of how refs are stored on disk.
The command that creates a new, empty Git repository in the current directory.
The command that reads and sets Git options, per repository or for your user, such as merge.conflictStyle or pull.rebase.
The command that prints an object in readable form: a commit with its diff, or a file at a given commit (git show A:path).
A command that reports how many loose objects the repository has and how much disk they use; -v adds pack details.
The command that copies a repository, including its history, into a new directory and sets the source up as the remote origin.
A clone that fetches only recent history (for example git clone --depth 1), so older commits and their objects are missing locally.
A clone that leaves out some objects, such as large blobs, and fetches them from the server only when needed (git clone --filter).
A Git object stored in its own zlib-compressed file under .git/objects, in a directory named after the first two hex characters of its hash. New objects are usually written loose and later packed.
A single file holding many Git objects, some stored as deltas against similar objects and all compressed. git gc creates them, and fetch, push and clone transfer them.
Storing one object as a list of differences from a similar base object instead of in full. Git uses it inside packfiles; it is a storage trick, separate from Git's snapshot model.
example: 1,000 versions of a 1 MB file with small edits can pack into a few MB.

definition: A widely used general-purpose data-compression library. Git compresses every object with it.
Git's housekeeping command: it packs loose objects into packfiles, packs refs and deletes unreachable objects older than a grace period. Git runs it automatically from time to time.
A Git object you can get to by starting from some ref (or a reflog entry) and following pointers. Garbage collection only ever deletes objects that are unreachable, and only after a grace period.
A local log of where each ref (including HEAD) has pointed over time. It keeps old commits reachable for a while, so it is the usual way to recover from a bad reset or rebase. It is never pushed.
example: git reflog shows HEAD@{1}: commit: copy, the commit before an amend.

definition: A ref Git sets to the previous branch tip before risky operations such as reset, merge and rebase, so you can get back. Later commands overwrite it.
How old an unreachable object must be before git gc deletes it; two weeks by default (gc.pruneExpire). git gc --prune=now removes them immediately.
A packfile in which git gc stores unreachable objects together with their ages, until they are old enough to prune.

A separately installed tool for rewriting a repository's entire history, for example to remove a committed secret or a huge file. Everyone must re-clone afterwards, and existing copies keep the old data.
Git Large File Storage: an extension that keeps large binary files on a separate server and stores only small pointer files in the repository.
A Git repository embedded inside another at a fixed commit. The outer tree records only that commit's hash, with mode 160000.
A file that just points to another path. Git stores the target path as a blob with mode 120000.
The file-permission flag that lets a file run as a program. It is the only permission Git tracks: mode 100755 instead of 100644.
A configured conversion Git applies when staging a file, so the stored blob differs from the bytes on disk; line-ending normalisation is the common example.
Converting Windows line endings (CR LF) to Unix ones (LF) when files are staged, and back on checkout if configured, so the repository stores one consistent form.
GNU Privacy Guard: free software implementing the OpenPGP standard for encryption and digital signatures. Git can use it, or SSH keys, to sign commits and tags.
Secure Shell: a protocol for encrypted remote login and command execution. Its key pairs are also used to authenticate to Git hosts and to sign commits and tags.
A commit or tag carrying a digital signature made with a GPG or SSH key. Because the hash covers all history, signing one hash vouches for everything behind it, if the hash resists collisions.
A credential that must stay private: an API key, password, token or private key. Once committed and pushed it should be treated as leaked and rotated.
Replacing a secret with a new one and revoking the old one, so a leaked copy stops working. It is the first response to a committed secret; rewriting history comes second.
A file listing patterns of untracked files Git should ignore, such as build output or .env. It has no effect on files already committed.
Apache Subversion: an older centralised version control system, where a branch is a copy of a directory on the central server.
The command that joins another branch's history into the current branch: a fast-forward if possible, otherwise a three-way merge that creates a merge commit. --no-ff always creates a merge commit.
The best common ancestor of two commits: the most recent commit both histories share. Git uses it as the 'base' in a three-way merge and in three-dot diffs.
example: For main A–B–E and feat A–B–C–D, the merge base is B.

definition: A commit that can be reached by following parents back from both of two commits.
A merge that compares three snapshots: the merge base, ours and theirs. A change made on only one side is taken; different changes to the same lines on both sides are a merge conflict.
A merge where the current branch is an ancestor of the other, so Git just moves the branch pointer forward and creates no new commit.
An update that would move a branch to a commit that does not contain its current tip, so commits would be dropped from its history. Git rejects such pushes unless forced.

Git's labels for the two sides of a conflict. In a merge, ours is the branch you are on and theirs is the branch being merged in; in a rebase they swap, because ours is the upstream plus already replayed commits.
Conflict-marker styles that also show the merge base's version between ||||||| and =======, so you can see what each side changed. zdiff3 trims lines common to both sides.
"Reuse recorded resolution": a Git feature that remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically when the same conflict appears again.
ort ("Ostensibly Recursive's Twin") is Git's default strategy for merging two branches since Git 2.34, a faster rewrite of the older recursive strategy.

Replaying a series of commits onto a new base commit, creating new commits with new hashes, then moving the branch to the last one. It gives linear history but rewrites commits, so it should not be used on commits others have built on.
example: git rebase main on feat replays C and D as C′ and D′ on top of main.

definition: A rebase that first opens a to-do list where you can reorder, edit, reword, squash, fixup or drop each commit; used to tidy a branch before review.
A commit made with git commit --fixup=<target>, titled fixup! plus the target's title. git rebase -i --autosquash moves it next to its target and melts it in.
A rebase form that replays only the commits after a given upstream onto a different new base: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream>.
Never rebase commits that other people have already pulled and built on: rewriting them makes histories diverge, with the same changes under different hashes.
History where every commit has exactly one parent, a straight line with no merge commits; produced by rebasing or squash merging.
The set of commits reachable from a commit by following parent pointers; commit X is an ancestor of Y if Y's history contains X.
A push that replaces the remote branch tip even when the new commit does not contain it, which can delete other people's commits from the branch. Needed after rewriting a pushed branch.
A safer force-push: it only overwrites the remote branch if it is still where your remote-tracking ref says, so an unseen push by someone else makes it fail as stale.

A push option (Git 2.30+) used with --force-with-lease that also checks the remote tip is reachable from your local branch's reflog, so a background fetch cannot make the lease pass for commits you never saw.
Integrating a branch by combining all its changes into one new commit with a single parent on the target branch. History stays linear, but the branch's commits do not become ancestors of the target.
Copying one commit's change onto the current branch as a new commit. Mostly used to backport fixes; -x records the original commit's hash in the message.
Applying a fix made on newer code to an older, still-supported release, usually by cherry-picking it onto the release branch.
Carrying a fix made on an older release branch forward into trunk so later releases include it. Fixing trunk first avoids needing it.
The command that creates a new commit undoing an earlier commit's change, leaving history intact; safe on shared branches. Reverting a merge needs -m 1 to name the mainline parent.
The command that moves the current branch to another commit; --hard also overwrites the staging area and working tree, discarding uncommitted changes.
The command that downloads new commits and objects from a remote and updates remote-tracking refs, without changing your branches.
git fetch followed by integrating the fetched branch into yours, by merge or by rebase depending on pull.rebase and pull.ff settings.
The command that uploads your commits to a remote and moves the remote branch, refusing non-fast-forward updates unless forced.
The remote branch a local branch tracks, used as the default for pull and push. In a rebase, the upstream is the branch you replay onto.
Two branches that each have commits the other lacks, so neither can simply fast-forward to the other; they need a merge or rebase.
Git's A..B notation. In git log it means commits reachable from B but not A; in git diff it simply compares tip A with tip B.
example: git log origin/main..main lists commits you have not pushed.

definition: Git's A...B notation. In git log it means commits on either side but not both (the symmetric difference); in git diff it compares the merge base with B, as pull request views do.
Finding an item in a sorted range by checking the middle and discarding the half that cannot contain it, repeatedly. It needs about log₂(n) steps for n items.
A commit whose change (diff) is identical to one already upstream, perhaps under a different hash after a cherry-pick. Rebase skips such commits.
A script Git runs automatically at a point in its workflow, such as before a commit is created (pre-commit). Teams use pre-commit hooks to run formatters and linters locally.
A team's agreement about which branches exist, how long they live and how work flows into the code that ships. GitHub flow, GitFlow and trunk-based development are the common ones.
How often each developer's work is combined with everyone else's. The less often, the bigger and riskier each integration.

Two changes that merge without any textual conflict but break each other's meaning, such as one changing what a function returns while another adds a caller expecting the old result. Only tests or review of the combined code can catch it.
The painful late phase of a project when long-separated pieces of work are finally combined and many conflicts and incompatibilities surface at once.
The single branch representing the current state of the product, usually called main, into which all work is integrated.
A branch where every commit builds and passes its tests, so it is a safe baseline for new work.
A branch for one piece of work, merged back into the mainline when finished. Short-lived ones (hours to days) keep integration easy.
A branch cut to stabilise and maintain one release. It receives only fixes, often cherry-picked from trunk, and is deleted when that release is no longer supported.
An urgent fix shipped straight to production outside the normal release schedule, such as v1.0.1 for a crash in v1.0.
A simple workflow: main is always deployable; each change gets a short-lived branch and a pull request with CI and review; it is merged into main and deployed.

Vincent Driessen's 2010 branching model with two permanent branches (main for releases, develop for integration) plus feature, release and hotfix branches. Suits explicitly versioned software; its author recommends simpler flows for continuously delivered web apps.
In GitFlow, the long-lived branch where finished features are integrated before a release branch is cut. It is a second integration point besides main.
A workflow where everyone integrates into one trunk at least daily, either directly or through branches lasting hours to a day or two, using feature flags to hide unfinished work.
DevOps Research and Assessment: a research programme, now part of Google Cloud, that has surveyed thousands of teams since 2014 to find which practices predict good software delivery performance.
A period when no new changes may be merged, usually before a release. DORA associates the absence of code freezes with higher delivery performance.

A runtime switch in the code that turns a behaviour on or off, for everyone or for a share of users, without redeploying. Lets unfinished work merge safely and separates deploy from release; each flag is debt to remove later.
Replacing a large component on trunk in small steps: put an interface in front of it, move callers to the interface, build the new implementation behind it, switch over, then delete the old one.
A 2012 trading-software failure in which a repurposed old flag reactivated dead code on one server; the SEC reported losses exceeding $460 million in about 45 minutes.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission, the regulator that investigated and published an account of the Knight Capital incident.
A workflow where contributors without push access copy (fork) the repository to their own account, push branches there and open pull requests against the original. Common in open source.

A request, on a hosting platform such as GitHub or GitLab, to merge a branch into another, where CI runs and colleagues review and discuss the change before it is merged. GitLab calls it a merge request.
A single repository holding many projects or services, often a whole company's code. Needs tools that build and test only what a change affects.
A branch per environment (dev, staging, prod) with code promoted by merging between them. An anti-pattern: the branches drift, so production runs code that was never tested as such.
Software a customer installs and runs on its own servers rather than using it as a hosted service, so several versions are often in use at once.
Software built into a hardware device, updated rarely and in discrete numbered versions.
A Git hosting platform owned by Microsoft, offering pull requests, code review, GitHub Actions CI and package hosting.
A Git hosting and DevOps platform offering merge requests, review and GitLab CI pipelines, available hosted or self-managed.
Atlassian's Git hosting platform, with pull requests and Bitbucket Pipelines CI.
How easy a codebase is to understand, change and keep correct. Google's review standard: approve a change once it definitely improves overall code health, even if it is not perfect.
A label for a minor, non-blocking review comment the author may take or leave, written as a Nit: prefix.
example: Nit: cfg → config would match the rest of this module.

definition: For your information: a review-comment prefix for something worth knowing that needs no action in this change.
Looks good to me: shorthand for approving a change in review.
A format for review comments that starts each with a label and optional decoration, such as suggestion:, question: or issue (blocking):, so their intent and severity are clear.
Rouan Wilsenach's model for sorting changes: Ship (merge directly), Show (open a pull request, merge once checks pass, invite feedback afterwards) and Ask (wait for review before merging).

Spending a disproportionate time arguing about trivial, easy-to-grasp details while important but harder questions go undiscussed. From Parkinson's example of a committee debating a bicycle shed instead of a reactor.
A series of small pull requests each built on the previous one, so later steps can be written and reviewed while earlier ones are still in review.
An attack where user input is pasted into an SQL string and changes the query's meaning. Prevented by passing values as query parameters instead of building SQL text.
example: An email of x' OR 1=1 -- can turn a lookup into a query returning every row.

definition: An SQL query with placeholders (such as ?) whose values are passed separately to the database driver, so input is always treated as data, never as SQL.
A Python bug pattern: a default value like [] is created once when the function is defined, so changes to it persist between calls. Use None and create the list inside. Ruff flags it as rule B006.
A bug where a loop or boundary is wrong by exactly one, such as using < instead of <=. Boundary tests catch them well.
A tool that rewrites code into one consistent layout automatically, ending style debates; Black and Ruff (Python), Prettier (JavaScript) and gofmt (Go) are examples.
A fast Python linter and code formatter, run as ruff check and ruff format.
Go's standard code formatter, which gives all Go code one layout.
Settings on GitHub or GitLab that restrict a branch, for example requiring approvals and passing status checks before merging, blocking force-pushes and dismissing stale approvals.
A pass or fail result that CI reports on a commit or pull request; branch protection can require named checks to pass before merging.
A review approval given before new commits were pushed, so it no longer covers the code that would merge. Branch protection can dismiss it automatically.
A file mapping path patterns to people or teams who own that code; on GitHub, the last matching pattern decides a file's owners, and branch protection can require an owner's approval.
Two people (or a whole group, in mob programming) writing code together at one screen, which reviews the code continuously as it is written.
A file recording the exact version of every dependency, including indirect ones, that was resolved, so later installs get the same versions.
A package your code depends on only indirectly, because one of your dependencies needs it.
Automatically searching commits and pushes for things that look like credentials, so leaks are caught or blocked.
Restricting which outside network addresses a system may connect to, so malicious code cannot easily send data out.
A tool that compares the versions of your dependencies with databases of known vulnerabilities and reports matches.
An SQL clause that locks the selected rows until the transaction ends, so two concurrent transactions cannot both read and change the same row.
The automated sequence of jobs (checkout, lint, test, build, scan, publish) that a CI system runs for every push or pull request, reporting pass or fail.
One unit of work in a CI pipeline, run on one runner; independent jobs can run in parallel.
A machine or container that executes CI jobs. Hosted runners are billed by the minute, so total compute is measured in runner-minutes.
GitHub's built-in CI/CD system: YAML workflow files in .github/workflows define jobs that run on runners in response to events such as push or pull_request. Reusable steps are called actions.
GitLab's built-in CI/CD system, configured by a .gitlab-ci.yml file in the repository.
A long-established open-source automation server, widely used to run CI pipelines.
A CI/CD service that orchestrates pipelines while the builds run on agents you host.
A hosted CI/CD service configured with a YAML file in the repository.
Analysing code to confirm values are used consistently with their declared types, before it runs; mypy and pyright do this for Python.
A short-lived access token GitHub Actions creates for each workflow run, with permissions set by the workflow's permissions key.
Giving each person, job or token only the permissions it needs and nothing more, to limit the damage if it is compromised.
A GitHub Actions setting that lets only one run with the same group name proceed at a time; with cancel-in-progress a new run cancels the one in progress.
A GitHub Actions job setting that fails the job after that many minutes; the default is 360.
A CI setting that runs the same job once for each combination of listed values, such as each supported Python version, in parallel.
The GitHub Actions trigger for pull request activity. It tests a temporary merge of the branch into the base, and runs from forks get read-only tokens and no secrets.
A GitHub Actions trigger that runs the base repository's workflow with its privileges and secrets for a pull request. Executing the pull request's own code under it is a known way to leak secrets.
The GitHub Actions event a merge queue sends when it wants the required checks run on a queued merge candidate.
Extreme Programming's target that the full build and tests finish in about ten minutes, fast enough for developers to wait for the result.
The name a CI cache is saved and restored under. Building it from a hash of the lockfile, OS and runtime version makes the cache refresh exactly when dependencies change.
Splitting a test suite into parts (shards) that run at the same time on separate machines, cutting waiting time at the price of more total compute.
Real elapsed time, as on a clock on the wall, as opposed to the total machine time spent across parallel workers.
Google's open-source build and test tool, designed for hermetic builds and for building only the targets affected by a change.
A build system for monorepos (Bazel, Nx, Pants, Turborepo) that works out which targets a change affects and builds and tests only those.
A system that tests each approved pull request on top of the latest main plus the pull requests ahead of it, and merges only if that combination passes, so main stays green under heavy traffic.
An open-source project gating system, created for the OpenStack project, that tests changes in the order they will merge.
An early merge-queue bot that tests the merged result of approved pull requests before merging them; the Rust project used a bors-style bot for years.
The packaged output of a build, such as a container image, Python wheel or binary, that gets tested and deployed. Build it once per commit and promote that same artefact through every environment.
A packaged, read-only file system plus settings from which containers are started; images are stored in registries and identified by tags and digests.
A server that stores and serves container images, such as Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry.
The content hash (for example sha256:…) that identifies one exact container image. Unlike a tag, it cannot be repointed.
The standard built-package format for Python (a .whl file), installable without a build step.
A build that depends only on its declared inputs, not on whatever happens to be installed on the machine.
A build where the same source, instructions and environment produce bit-for-bit identical output, so anyone can check a published binary matches its source.
Verifiable metadata stating which source, build process and inputs produced an artefact.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a framework of increasing levels of build integrity, including signed provenance.
OpenID Connect: an identity layer on OAuth 2.0. CI systems use it to swap a short-lived signed token for temporary cloud credentials, avoiding long-lived stored secrets.
A March 2025 supply-chain attack in which the version tags of a popular GitHub Action were repointed to a malicious commit that printed CI secrets into workflow logs (CVE-2025-30066).
An attack that compromises something you depend on, such as a library, build tool or CI action, to reach you through it.
Referring to a GitHub Action by its full 40-character commit hash instead of a tag, so a moved tag cannot change the code you run.
GitHub's tool that opens pull requests to update dependencies and action pins, and alerts on known-vulnerable versions.
A file of named tasks and their commands, run with the make tool; often used so developers and CI run identical commands.
A tool that runs named project tasks (test, lint, build) the same way everywhere; make, tox and nox are examples.
A Python tool that runs tests and other tasks in freshly created virtual environments, often for several Python versions.
A Python task runner like tox, configured in Python code (noxfile.py).
Python's standard package installer; requirements.txt is a plain list of packages for it to install.
A framework for managing Git pre-commit hooks, commonly used to run formatters and linters before each commit.
Keeping software always in a releasable state, so any change that passes the pipeline could go to production on demand; a person may still choose when.
Sending every change that passes the pipeline to production automatically, with no human gate. It requires continuous delivery.
Putting a new version of the software onto production machines. It need not change what users see, if the new behaviour is behind a feature flag; exposing it is the release.
Exposing new behaviour to users, for example by turning a feature flag on. With flags, release can happen separately from, and after, deployment.
Running a new code path in production on real traffic while discarding or only logging its result, to check performance and correctness before anyone sees it.
The automated path a change takes from commit to production: build, tests, staging and a gated, monitored production rollout, with the same artefact at every stage.
Exposing a new version to more and more traffic in stages, checking health at each stage, so a bad version affects few users.
A rollout that stops all old instances before starting new ones; simple, but causes downtime.
A rollout that replaces instances a few at a time, so old and new versions serve traffic together for a while and must be compatible.

Running two full production environments: one (blue) serves traffic while the new version is deployed to the other (green) and tested; the router then switches over, and switching back is the rollback.
Sending a small share of traffic (say 1%) to a new version and comparing its health with the old version before expanding. Named after canaries once used to detect gas in mines.
Instances of the old version running at the same scale and time as the canary, used for a fair comparison that ordinary daily variation cannot distort.
An open-source system for running containers across a cluster of machines; its Deployment object performs rolling updates by default.
The response time that 99% of requests beat; it shows how slow the slowest 1% are, which averages hide.
How full a service's most constrained resource is (CPU, memory, connections); one of the signals SRE teams watch during rollouts.
A measure of traffic: how many requests a service receives each second.
The fraction of requests that fail, such as 0.1% (1 in 1,000).
The probability distribution of how many rare, independent events happen in a fixed interval. If you expect λ events, the typical random spread is about the square root of λ.
example: Expecting 6 errors, seeing anything from about 3 to 9 is unremarkable.

definition: The probability that a test detects a real effect of a given size. A small canary sample has little power to notice a modest rise in a rare error rate.
Artificial requests generated on purpose to exercise a service, used when real traffic is too low to give a signal.

Undoing a change to return to the previous good state. For a deployment, it means redeploying the previous artefact (or switching traffic back): usually the fastest fix, but only safe if the old version still works with the current data and schema. In a database, a transaction rollback discards that transaction's uncommitted changes.
Recovering from a bad deployment by shipping a fix rather than going back to the previous version.
An unplanned event that disrupts or degrades a live service for users.
A scripted change to a database's structure, such as adding or dropping a column. Destructive ones cannot be undone by rolling back code.
A database column that may hold NULL (no value), so existing rows and old code that never set it stay valid.
Filling a newly added column or table with values for existing rows, usually in small batches to avoid long locks.
During a migration, having the code write the same data to both the old and the new column so either can be read.
The SQL statement that changes an existing table's structure, such as adding, renaming or dropping columns.
Extra information after a plus sign in a SemVer version, such as 1.0.0+20260101; it is ignored when ordering versions.
The rule that decides which of two versions counts as newer, comparing major, minor and patch numbers, then pre-release identifiers piece by piece.
A rule in a dependency declaration that accepts a set of versions rather than one, such as ^1.2.3.
An npm range like ^1.2.3 that accepts updates which do not change the left-most non-zero number: >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, but only >=0.2.3 <0.3.0 for ^0.2.3.
An npm range like ~1.2.3 that accepts patch updates only: >=1.2.3 <1.3.0.
The package manager for JavaScript and Node.js; package.json declares a project's dependencies and npx runs a package's command.
npm's library and command-line tool implementing SemVer comparison and range matching.
Versioning by release date, such as Ubuntu 24.04 for April 2024.
A popular Linux distribution, released every six months with versions named by year and month.
A commit-message convention with a machine-readable prefix such as fix:, feat: or feat!:, so tools can derive version bumps and release notes.
In Conventional Commits, a BREAKING CHANGE: line at the end of the message (or a ! after the type) marking a change that requires a MAJOR version bump.
A tool that reads Conventional Commits, works out the next version, and publishes the release, notes and packages through plugins.
Google's tool that reads Conventional Commits and opens a release pull request; merging it creates the tag and GitHub release.
A human-readable list of notable changes in each release.
A command that names a commit relative to the nearest annotated tag, as tag-commits-ghash, for example v2.1.0-10-gefb7ccd. --tags lets it use lightweight tags.

DORA's five measures of delivery performance: change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time (the DORA throughput metrics), and change fail rate and deployment rework rate (the DORA instability metrics).
The time from a change being committed to it running in production; a DORA throughput metric.
How often a team deploys to production; a DORA throughput metric.
How long it takes to recover after a deployment causes a failure in production; a DORA throughput metric, formerly called time to restore service.
The share of deployments that need immediate intervention, such as a rollback or hotfix; a DORA instability metric.
The share of deployments that were unplanned and made because of a production incident; a DORA instability metric added in 2024.
Shipping weeks or months of changes in one go, so any failure is hard to trace to its cause.
One of DORA's three measures of how quickly changes move through delivery: change lead time, deployment frequency and failed deployment recovery time.
One of DORA's two measures of how often deployments go wrong: change fail rate and deployment rework rate. Unrelated to the package-instability metric used in software design.
The lines <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> (plus ||||||| in diff3 style) that Git writes into a file to show both sides of a merge conflict for you to resolve.
Approving a code review without really reading or understanding the change, so the review adds a sign-off but catches nothing.

A code-review anti-pattern where review becomes a barrier instead of help: one person must approve everything and becomes a bottleneck, or reviewers block on personal preference or leave reviews waiting for days.
